label: Person
name: Martin Luther
summary:
Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German Augustinian friar whose Ninety-Five Theses (1517), doctrine of justification by faith alone, and German Bible translation ignited the Protestant Reformation — the most consequential schism in Western Christianity.

Tormented by divine righteousness, he experienced his 'Tower Experience' (c. 1515) — the revelation that salvation comes through faith, not works. On October 31, 1517, he challenged the sale of indulgences, and Gutenberg's press spread his protest across Europe within weeks.

At the Diet of Worms (1521), he refused to recant: 'Here I stand; I can do no other.' In Wartburg Castle he translated the New Testament into German in 11 weeks — a literary masterpiece that standardized the German language.

His five solas catalyzed all Protestant churches and indirectly contributed to the Wars of Religion, the Peace of Westphalia, sovereign nation-states, and the Enlightenment's emphasis on individual conscience.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Martin Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and subsequent actions catalyzed the Protestant Reformation, leading to a schism that split Western Christianity into two major branches. The movement had an estimated 50-100 million adherents by the mid-16th century.
